sections.title: When a Minor's Obligation Starts and the Nature of Chinukh
sections.gist: Beit Shammai set the line at a child who can ride on his father's shoulders, Beit Hillel at one who can walk up holding his hand. Abaye adds that the mitzvah of *chinukh* follows what an adult in the child's condition would owe.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Beit Shammai): a *katan* who can't ride on his father's shoulders from Jerusalem up to the Temple Mount is exempt. The test is what the child can manage, not his age.
R. Zeira objects: the test covers only the climb from Jerusalem, so who brought him as far as Jerusalem?

Abaye: his mother did. She is obligated in *simchah*, so she comes to Jerusalem anyway and brings him with her, and the father's duty starts only from there. By Beit Hillel's standard, a child who can walk up holding his father's hand is obligated.

Rebbi supports Beit Hillel from Chana, who kept Shmuel home "until the child is weaned" (I Shmuel 1:22). Shmuel could already ride on shoulders, so if that were the standard, she would have brought him.
His father rejects the proof. Chana herself was obligated in *simchah* and still stayed home, so her reason was personal: Shmuel was delicate and couldn't make the trip.
R. Shimon asks about a lame child, who can be carried (a question for Beit Shammai), and a blind child, who can be led (a question for both schools).
The question is only about a child who may heal. A permanently disabled child will be exempt as an adult too, so there is nothing to train him for.

Abaye: *chinukh* follows what an adult in the same condition owes now. A lame or blind adult is exempt, so the child is exempt too, even if he may recover, since the mitzvah of *chinukh* prepares a child for a duty, and in his present state there is none.

sections.title: Which Has the Higher Minimum: Olat Re'iyah or Shalmei Chagigah?
sections.gist: Which festival offering has the higher minimum, and, underneath that dispute, what the *olah* brought at Sinai was.

children.title: Why Beit Shammai Favor the Olah and Beit Hillel the Shelamim
children.gist: Beit Shammai give the *re'iyah* the higher minimum and Beit Hillel the *chagigah*. Each school brings two arguments and answers the other's, until the dispute turns on what was offered at Sinai.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai: the *olat re'iyah* costs at least two silver *kesef* and the *shalmei chagigah* at least one *ma'ah*. Beit Hillel reverse the two.

Beneath the numbers is a question of emphasis. Beit Shammai favor the *olah*, which is God's alone; Beit Hillel favor the *shelamim*, which God and the worshipper share. At stake is how much the human side counts in worship.
Beit Hillel argue that the *shelamim* came first: Shemot 24:5, "*vayizbechu zevachim shelamim*", shows the *chagigah* type offered before *matan Torah*, which gives it the greater weight.
Beit Shammai answer from the same verse, "*vaya'alu olot*": the *olah* was offered before Sinai as well, so that argument favors neither side.

So the dispute becomes what those Sinai *olot* were. Beit Hillel say the *olat tamid*, a communal offering, which proves nothing about an individual's *re'iyah*. Beit Shammai say an *olat re'iyah*, the very offering in question.
It is striking that both sides treat practice before Sinai as binding precedent at all, when events before *matan Torah* usually carry no legal weight.

rows:
1. The *olah* goes entirely to God
2. Shavuot's offerings have more *olot* than *shelamim*

1. The *shelamim* has two "eatings": the altar and the owner
2. Shavuot's are communal; learn an individual's offering from individuals

1. The *chagigah* existed before the *dibbur* (Shemot 24:5)
2. The *nesi'im* brought more *shelamim* than *olot*

1. The *olah* also existed before the *dibbur*
2. The *nesi'im* brought theirs once; learn from what applies in every generation

children.title: What Was the Olah Offered at Sinai?
children.gist: Abaye lines up six *tanna'im* in two camps on what the Sinai *olah* was, three for an *olat re'iyah* and three for the *olat tamid*. The Gemara tests the reason he gives for each and ends by striking R. Yishmael from the list.

children.title: Abaye: Six Tanna'im in Two Camps
children.gist: Abaye divides six *tanna'im* into two camps. Beit Shammai, R. Elazar and R. Yishmael say the Sinai *olah* was an *olat re'iyah*; Beit Hillel, R. Akiva and R. Yosi HaGlili say it was the *olat tamid*, each for a reason of his own.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai, R. Elazar and R. Yishmael: the Sinai *olah* was an *olat re'iyah*, an individual's offering.
Beit Hillel, R. Akiva and R. Yosi HaGlili: it was the *olat tamid*, the daily communal offering. The chart gives each one's reason.

rows: The *tamid* was commanded at Sinai but not offered there
Olat re'iyah (later struck from the list)
*Pratot* came only at the Ohel Mo'ed, so no *tamid* without *hefshet*
Offered at Sinai and never interrupted

children.title: R. Yishmael vs. R. Akiva: Were the Details of the Mitzvot Given at Sinai?
children.gist: R. Yishmael holds that the general rules came at Sinai and the details only later, placing him with Beit Shammai. R. Akiva holds that rules and details were both given at Sinai.

bullets.text: R. Yishmael: *kelalot ne'emru be'Sinai, u'feratot be'Ohel Mo'ed*. The general rules were said at Sinai and the details at the Ohel Mo'ed.

So a Sinai *tamid* would have been offered without *hefshet ve'nituach*, which became required only later. A *tamid* whose rules changed seems impossible, so for R. Yishmael the Sinai *olah* must have been a *re'iyah*.
R. Akiva: the rules and the details were both given at Sinai, repeated at the Ohel Mo'ed, and taught a third time in Arvot Mo'av.
The positions look inverted. R. Akiva derives laws from every letter, while R. Yishmael holds *dibrah Torah kilshon benei adam* (the Torah speaks in human language).
A resolution: for R. Akiva, details "given at Sinai" means encoded in the text for the Sages to derive. For R. Yishmael, details count as given only once they are stated explicitly.

illustration.caption: R. Yishmael and R. Akiva disagree on when the details of the mitzvot were given. For R. Yishmael, a *tamid* offered at Sinai would have come before the laws of *hefshet ve'nituach* were given.

children.title: When Did the Tamid Begin?
children.gist: The Gemara explains why R. Yishmael can't say the Sinai *olah* was a *tamid*. R. Elazar and R. Akiva then disagree on whether the *tamid* was offered at Sinai at all, or only from the Mishkan on.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: is there anything that at first didn't need *hefshet ve'nituach* and later did? There isn't, so for R. Yishmael the Sinai *olah* must have been a *re'iyah*.
Tosafot: *hefshet ve'nituach* is written in the *tamid*'s own *parashah*, so a *tamid* whose rules changed would be especially hard to accept. A private *olah* would be less of a problem.

R. Elazar reads "*olat tamid ha'asuyah be'Har Sinai*" (Bamidbar 28:6) as describing its procedures: they were told at Sinai, but the *tamid* wasn't offered until the Mishkan. So the Sinai *olah* was a *re'iyah*.
R. Akiva reads the verse literally: the *tamid* was offered at Sinai and never stopped.
Amos 5:25 seems to challenge him: "Did you bring Me sacrifices… forty years in the wilderness?"
The answer: *shevet Levi*, who didn't worship the calf, offered it from their own funds, so the nation as a whole didn't.
The verse is odd on any view. Even for R. Elazar, the *tamid* ran from the second year, so for thirty-nine years at least.

children.title: R. Yosi HaGlili: What Each Pilgrimage Offering Has Alone
children.gist: Three pilgrimage offerings, each with its own unique feature. Since only the *chagigah* preceded Sinai, the Sinai *olah* must have been the *tamid*.

bullets.text: R. Yosi HaGlili: the *re'iyah*, the *chagigah* and the *simchah* each have something the other two lack.
The *chagigah*'s distinction is that it existed before *matan Torah*, the same fact Beit Hillel rely on.
That means the *re'iyah* did not precede Sinai, so the *olah* in Shemot 24 was the *olat tamid*.
Open question: why call the Sinai *shelamim* a *chagigah* and not a *simchah*? The Gemara doesn't say.

rows: Goes entirely to God; the other two are mostly eaten
Obligates women as well as men

children.title: The Gemara Strikes R. Yishmael from Abaye's List
children.gist: R. Yosi HaGlili's own *baraita* undercuts Abaye's reasoning about R. Yishmael, so the Gemara strikes R. Yishmael from the list.

bullets.text: Why did Abaye put R. Yishmael with Beit Shammai? Only because of the *hefshet ve'nituach* argument.

But R. Yosi HaGlili holds both that the Sinai *olah* was a *tamid* and that it needed no *hefshet ve'nituach*, a requirement that began at the Ohel Mo'ed. So a *tamid* whose rules changed is a coherent position.
Nothing then forces R. Yishmael's view either way, so the Gemara deletes him from Abaye's list.
Beit Shammai's reading makes Sinai a moment of encounter with God. Beit Hillel's makes it the quiet daily *tamid*: worship as steady routine.

returns_to.note: Revisits Abaye's placement of R. Yishmael

children.title: Were the Sinai Olot Bulls Too?
children.gist: Rav Chisda asks whether "bulls" in Shemot 24:5 describes both the *olot* and the *shelamim* or only the *shelamim*. The question is left unresolved.

bullets.text: Rav Chisda: is there a break after "*vaya'alu olot*"? Then the *olot* were sheep and only the *shelamim* were bulls. Or does "bulls" describe both?
Mar Zutra: the difference is where the cantillation places its break in the verse.
Rav Acha b. Rava: it decides what to bring for one who vows "an *olah* like the one at Sinai", a bull or a sheep.
*Teiku*: the question stands.

returns_to.note: Returns to Shemot 24:5, the verse both schools cited

sections.title: Does the Re'iyah Have No Minimum, or Only No Maximum?
sections.gist: If the *re'iyah* has a minimum cost, how can the Mishnah in Pe'ah list it among the mitzvot with no measure? The answer depends on what "no measure" rules out, a floor, a ceiling or both, which the Gemara takes up on 7a.

bullets.text: Pe'ah 1:1: "These have no measure: *pe'ah*, *bikkurim*, *re'ayon*, *gemilut chasadim* and Torah study."
Does "no measure" rule out a floor, a ceiling or both? Compare the Yerushalmi on *pe'ah*, and R. Yochanan's view that one may make a whole field *bikkurim*.

sections.continues: Continues on 7a: R. Yochanan's first reading, R. Oshaya's correction, and R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on *re'ayon*.

judgment_calls: R. Yosi HaGlili's three offerings is conceptually self-contained and could be its own top-level section; kept under the Sinai debate because the Gemara cites it as the source for his position there.
Rabbi Yishmael Realigned returns to the Positions subsection; kept in Gemara order with a returns_to link rather than moved.
Parsing the Verse could sit under the Beit Hillel / Beit Shammai reasons (it returns to their verse); kept as the last step of the Sinai debate, where it falls in the text.
coverage_notes: The minor's-obligation exchange (5b–6a) isn't discussed in this shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only.
The essay says the Gemara 'reassigns R. Yishmael to Beit Hillel'; the text only deletes him from Abaye's list. Followed the text.
The segmentation names R. Eliezer where the text has R. Elazar. Followed the text.
The shiur continues into 7a (re'iyah without a measure; R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish); outside this daf's scope.

quiz.q: By Beit Shammai's standard, which child must his father bring up to the Temple?
options: One who can ride on his father's shoulders from Jerusalem to the Temple Mount
One who can walk up holding his father's hand
Any child who has reached the age of *chinukh*
Only a child who has reached thirteen
quiz.why: The test is what the child can manage. Beit Hillel's line is lower: a child who can walk up holding his father's hand.

quiz.q: If the Mishnah's test covers only the climb from Jerusalem, who brings the child as far as Jerusalem (Abaye)?
options: His mother, who comes anyway because she is obligated in *simchah*
His father, as part of *chinukh*
No one: he must walk the whole way
The kohanim
quiz.why: Her obligation in *simchah* brings her and the child to Jerusalem, so the father's duty starts only from there.

quiz.q: Must a father bring a lame child who may yet heal (Abaye)?
options: No: *chinukh* follows what an adult in the same condition owes now
Yes, since he will be obligated once he heals
Yes, if someone can carry him
Only by Beit Hillel
quiz.why: A lame adult is exempt, and the mitzvah of *chinukh* prepares a child for a duty he would have in his present state.

quiz.q: Why do Beit Hillel give the *shalmei chagigah* the higher minimum?
options: It was offered before the Torah was given, and it is shared by God and the worshipper
It is burned entirely for God
More of them were brought on Shavuot
Women are obligated in it
quiz.why: Shemot 24:5 shows *shelamim* before Sinai; the shiur adds that Beit Hillel favor the offering that God and the person share.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, how do R. Akiva and R. Yosi HaGlili identify the *olah* offered at Sinai?
options: As the *olat tamid*
As an *olat re'iyah*
As a *chagigah*
They leave it unresolved
quiz.why: Abaye places them with Beit Hillel; Beit Shammai, R. Elazar and R. Yishmael say it was an *olat re'iyah*.

quiz.q: Why did Abaye first place R. Yishmael with Beit Shammai?
options: For R. Yishmael the details came later, so a Sinai *tamid* would have lacked *hefshet ve'nituach*
R. Yishmael was a student of Beit Shammai
R. Yishmael says the Torah speaks in human language
R. Yishmael says the *tamid* was never interrupted
quiz.why: *Kelalot be'Sinai, u'feratot be'Ohel Mo'ed*: a *tamid* whose rules later changed seemed impossible.

quiz.q: What does R. Yosi HaGlili say only the *shalmei chagigah* has?
options: It existed before the Torah was given
It obligates women as well as men
It goes entirely to God
It has no fixed measure
quiz.why: The *simchah* obligates women and the *re'iyah* goes entirely to God; the *chagigah* alone preceded Sinai.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara strike R. Yishmael from Abaye's list?
options: R. Yosi HaGlili holds a Sinai *tamid* without *hefshet ve'nituach*, so that view is coherent
R. Yishmael retracted his view
R. Akiva refuted him
The verse in Amos contradicts him
quiz.why: Abaye's only reason for placing him falls away, so nothing decides which camp he belongs in.
